derivations.claim: If $Z$ has finite range $z_1,\ldots,z_m\in C$ with probabilities $p_1,\ldots,p_m$, then [F3] gives $\mathbb E Z=\sum_i p_i z_i$, a convex combination in $C$. Joint convexity proves $\psi(\mathbb E Z)\le\sum_i p_i\psi(z_i)=\mathbb E\psi(Z)$ by induction on the number of positive weights: combine the first $m-1$ points into their normalized convex average, apply the induction hypothesis, then apply two-point convexity with weights $1-p_m$ and $p_m$.

For $n\ge1$ set $D_n=\{(m_1/n,\ldots,m_K/n):m_i\in\mathbb N_0,\sum_i m_i=n\}\subseteq\Delta_K$. This is a finite set with a canonical lexicographic order. For $p\in\Delta_K$, put $m_i=\lfloor np_i\rfloor$ for $i<K$ and $m_K=n-\sum_{i<K}m_i$. Then $m_K\ge0$, the coordinates sum to $n$, and the first $K-1$ coordinate errors are below $1/n$ while the last is below $(K-1)/n$. Thus some $q\in D_n$ has $\|p-q\|_2<\sqrt{K(K-1)}/n$. The product grid $D_n\times D_n$ therefore approximates every point of $C$ within $2K/n$. List its finitely many points canonically as $c_{n,1},\ldots,c_{n,m_n}$ and assign each point of $C$ to the first ball of radius $2K/n$ containing it. The cells are Borel by [F5]; replacing $Z$ on each cell by its center defines a measurable finite-range $Z_n\in C$ with $\|Z_n-Z\|_2<2K/n$ everywhere. The grid, order and assignment are explicit, so no choice axiom is used.

Step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E Z_n\in C$ for every $n$. Each coordinate of $Z_n$ and $Z$ is bounded by $1$, so dominated convergence [F4] gives $\mathbb E Z_n\to\mathbb E Z$ coordinatewise; because the coordinate constraints defining $C$ are closed, $\mathbb E Z\in C$.

By [F2], $\psi$ is uniformly continuous on $C$. Choose $\delta>0$ so that points within distance $\delta$ have $\psi$-values within $1$, and then choose $n$ with $2K/n<\delta$. The finite grid in step 1.2 is a $\delta$-net, so $|\psi(z)|\le1+\max_{c\in D_n\times D_n}|\psi(c)|$ for every $z\in C$. This is a common finite bound. Since $\|Z_n-Z\|_2\to0$, continuity gives $\psi(Z_n)\to\psi(Z)$ pointwise; [F4] then gives $\mathbb E\psi(Z_n)\to\mathbb E\psi(Z)$.
Applying step 1.1 to each $Z_n$ gives $\psi(\mathbb E Z_n)\le\mathbb E\psi(Z_n)$. By continuity of $\psi$ and steps 2.1 and 2.2, taking limits proves $\psi(\mathbb E Z)\le\mathbb E\psi(Z)$.

derivations.claim: For each $j$, choose a version $Z_j$ of $\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{Y=y_j\}}\mid\mathcal G]$, which exists by [A1,F1]. Order preservation and preservation of constants give $0\le Z_j\le1$ almost surely by [F2]. Set $N_j=\{Z_j<0\}\cup\{Z_j>1\}\in\mathcal G$ and $Z'_j=Z_j\mathbf1_{N_j^c}$. Then $Z'_j$ is $\mathcal G$-measurable, takes values in $[0,1]$ everywhere, and equals $Z_j$ almost surely. By [F3], it has the same event integrals, so it remains a conditional-expectation version. Linearity shows that $\sum_jZ_j$ is a version of the conditional expectation of $\sum_j\mathbf1_{\{Y=y_j\}}=1$; the constant 1 is another version, so [F6] gives $\sum_jZ_j=1$ almost surely. Hence $\sum_jZ'_j=1$ almost surely.

For each label $j$ and rational $q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$, the event $\{Z'_j<q\}\in\mathcal G$ equals $X^{-1}(A_{j,q})$ for some $A_{j,q}\in\Sigma_X$ by [F5]. AC permits choosing these sets for the countable family of label-rational pairs. Define $\tilde\eta_j(x)=\inf(\{q\in\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]:x\in A_{j,q}\}\cup\{1\})$. For $0<t\le1$, $\{x:\tilde\eta_j(x)<t\}=\bigcup_{q<t}A_{j,q}$; for $t\le0$ this sublevel set is empty and for $t>1$ it is all of $\mathsf X$. Thus each $\tilde\eta_j$ is measurable and takes values in $[0,1]$ by [F4,F7].

For every $j$ and $\omega$, the rationals $q$ satisfying $X(\omega)\in A_{j,q}$ are exactly those with $Z'_j(\omega)<q$. Their infimum is $Z'_j(\omega)$ when this value is below $1$; at value $1$ the rational set is empty and the filler $1$ gives the same value. Thus $\tilde\eta_j(X)=Z'_j$ everywhere. The measurable set $D=\{x:\sum_j\tilde\eta_j(x)=1\}$ is well-defined by [F7]. Define $\eta(x)=(\tilde\eta_1(x),\ldots,\tilde\eta_K(x))$ on $D$ and $\eta(x)=(1,0,\ldots,0)$ off $D$. Then $\eta$ is measurable, takes values in $\Delta_K$ everywhere, and $\eta_j(X)=Z'_j$ almost surely because $\sum_jZ'_j=1$ almost surely.

For every $A\in\Sigma_X$ and label index $j$, the event $\{X\in A\}$ belongs to $\mathcal G$. The conditional-expectation identity [F1] and almost-sure equality [F3] therefore give $P(X\in A,Y=y_j)=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{X\in A\}}Z_j]=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{X\in A\}}Z'_j]=\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{X\in A\}}\eta_j(X)].$ This is the claimed event identity for every class.

Otherwise $q_j>0$ for every $j$ with $p_j>0$. The truthful risk is finite, and cancellation on the support of $p$ gives $\bar S_{\log}(p,q)-\bar S_{\log}(p,p)=\sum_{j:p_j>0}p_j\log\frac{p_j}{q_j}.$ Applying step 1.1 to $t=q_j/p_j$ yields $\sum_{j:p_j>0}p_j\log\frac{p_j}{q_j}\ge 1-\sum_{j:p_j>0}q_j\ge0.$ If the displayed difference is zero, both nonnegative gaps in this chain are zero. Equality in step 1.1 then forces $q_j/p_j=1$ on the support of $p$, and the second gap forces $q$ to have no mass outside that support. Hence $q=p$. derivations.claim: By [F1], choose a measurable posterior probability kernel $\Pi_x$ on the finite label set; identify it with the measurable vector $G(x)=(\Pi_x(1),\ldots,\Pi_x(K))\in\Delta_K$. For each $x$, the posterior expected score of reporting $q$ is $\bar S(G(x),q)$, which is minimized at $q=G(x)$ by [F2]. The posterior risk of this rule is measurable by [F4], so the rule meets the measurable-minimizer hypothesis in [F6].

To apply the Bayes-risk interface to the original joint law, let $\pi_j=P(Y=j)$. For $\pi_j>0$, define $K_j(A)=P(X\in A,Y=j)/\pi_j$ on feature events $A$; for $\pi_j=0$, set $K_j=P_X$. Each $K_j$ is a probability measure, and the finite map $j\mapsto K_j$ is a probability kernel. The joint prior-data law built from prior $(\pi_j)$ and kernel $K_j$ agrees with the original joint law because for every $A$ and $j$ its $(A,j)$ mass is $P(X\in A,Y=j)$, including zero-prior labels. Consequently the Bayes-risk theorem [F6] states that the posterior rule $G$ minimizes the original expected score risk over all measurable randomized forecasts, hence over deterministic forecasts.

Now suppose $S$ is strictly proper and another measurable forecast $q$ has the same risk as $G$, whose risk is finite by hypothesis. The posterior disintegration identity writes their risk difference as $\mathbb E\big[\bar S(G(X),q(X))-\bar S(G(X),G(X))\big]=0.$ Each nonnegative posterior-risk term is finite almost surely because its expectation is finite. Thus the integrand is a well-defined measurable nonnegative difference by [F3,F4], and [F5] makes it zero almost surely. Strict propriety in [F2] then gives $q(X)=G(X)$ almost surely.

If $a>1/2$ then $u\le0$, so monotonicity gives $\Phi(-u)-\Phi(u)\ge0$; if $a<1/2$ then $u\ge0$, so $\Phi(-u)-\Phi(u)\le0$. In each model the three forecast vectors are distinct. Therefore full reliability would require $p_i=g_i$ at every row by [F1], but Model A row 1, Model B row 1, and Model C row 1 each have $p_i\ne g_i$. Full reliability fails in all three models.

In Model A, for each label the groups with forecast coordinate $0.4$ have conditional frequency $0.4$, and the groups with coordinate $0.3$ have average conditional frequency $0.3$: for labels 1, 2, and 3 the latter averages are respectively $(0.2+0.4)/2$, $(0.4+0.2)/2$, and $(0.2+0.4)/2$. Thus Model A is classwise calibrated. Its top confidence is always $0.4$, its predicted labels are $1,2,3$ in the three rows, and each corresponding conditional correctness probability is $0.4$, so it is top-confidence calibrated.

In Model B the top confidence is always $0.5$, the predicted labels are $1,2,3$, and the average conditional correctness is $(0.7+0.5+0.3)/3=0.5$, so top-confidence calibration holds. Classwise calibration fails because forecast coordinate $G_1=0.5$ occurs only in row 1, where $P(Y=1\mid X=1)=0.7\ne0.5$.

In Model C, for each label the forecast coordinate $0.5$ group has average conditional frequency $0.5$, and the coordinate $0$ group has frequency $0$: the three nonzero-group averages are $(0.8+0.2)/2$, $(0.2+0.8)/2$, and $(0.8+0.2)/2$. Thus classwise calibration holds. All top confidences equal $0.5$; the tie-broken predicted labels are $1,1,2$, with conditional correctness probabilities $0.8,0.2,0.8$. Their average is $0.6\ne0.5$, so top-confidence calibration fails. Steps 1.1, 1.2, and 1.3 establish the other model claims; the Model C calculation completes the pairwise distinctions.
